drafts.P8092:
The Alaska Natural Gas Development Authority is a public corporation of the State of Alaska. Ballot Measure 3 of the 2002 election established it.{a0_1} It filed an application dated April 4, 2005 for a conditional use right-of-way lease for the spur line. The line would connect Glennallen to the Cook Inlet gas distribution system.{a0_1}

The route would start at the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System corridor near Glennallen. The first 15 miles would cross Ahtna lands. The line would then follow the Glenn Highway right-of-way for almost 50 miles. From Chickaloon to Palmer it would mostly follow an existing Matanuska Electric Association route.{a0_1} No report of construction or a start date has been found.
drafts.P8106:
Xcel Energy opened the pipeline in October 2014. It carries gas from Fort Lupton to the Cherokee power plant near Commerce City.{a0_2}

The pipeline was part of Xcel's plan to comply with the 2010 Clean Air Clean Jobs Act. The act required Xcel and other power companies to cut nitrous oxide emissions by up to 80 percent at several coal-fired plants by 2017.{a0_2} The line cost $110 million. It crosses under the South Platte River, nine canals and three major roadways.{a0_2}
drafts.P8131:
WBI Energy began the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission pre-filing process for the project in June 2015. The pipeline would have supplied 221.5 MMcf/d of capacity to the Demicks Lake gas plant that ONEOK Rockies Midstream proposed west of Keene.{a0_3}

The Energy Information Administration listed the project as cancelled in its August 2018 release, under docket PF15-24.{a0_4}
drafts.P8144:
Egan Hub Storage LLC is a subsidiary of Spectra Energy. In October 2007 the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued it a certificate to add a fourth salt dome storage cavern at its Acadia Parish facility. The project included a 24-inch loop of the Line 73 header, a new meter and regulating station for Texas Gas Transmission, and an upgrade to a Texas Eastern Transmission station.{a0_5} When completed, the storage site would have an overall capacity of 42 Bcf.{a0_5}

In September 2010 the Commission authorized the remaining 8.5 miles of header pipeline. This made the header system 16.5 miles long.{a0_6}
drafts.P8166:
Gill Ranch Storage LLC and Pacific Gas and Electric Company applied to the California Public Utilities Commission on July 29, 2008 to build the Gill Ranch Gas Storage Project. It included a 20 billion cubic foot storage field, a compressor station and a natural gas pipeline.{a0_7} The pipeline would run between the utility's existing Line 401 near Interstate 5 and the compressor site in western Madera County.{a0_7}

The applicants said the project would add storage in the southern San Joaquin Valley, close to the utility's existing gas and electric facilities.{a0_7} The Energy Information Administration lists the lateral as completed in November 2010.{a0_8}
drafts.P8181:
Houston Pipe Line Company, a unit of Energy Transfer Partners, received approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in March 2014 to build the extension. It would export natural gas to northern Mexico and supply industrial users and power plants near Reynosa.{a0_9} The line would cross under the Rio Grande and connect to a Pemex pipeline on the Mexican side.{a0_9} Supplies would be mostly Texas gas.{a0_9}

In a notice dated December 26, 2013, Commission staff said it would prepare an environmental assessment of the border crossing project.{a0_10} The Energy Information Administration lists the project as in service on June 8, 2015.{a0_8}
drafts.P8195:
Central New York Oil and Gas Company, LLC applied to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission under docket CP10-480. The project also included two compressor installations and two meter stations. Commission staff published its environmental assessment in June 2011.{a0_12} The Commission approved the project in November 2011.{a0_11}

The line connects to Tennessee Gas Pipeline's Line 300, to Transcontinental Gas Pipe Line's Leidy Line, and to Stagecoach storage laterals that tie in with Millennium Pipeline. It was meant to carry gas from northeastern Pennsylvania to the Stagecoach Gas Storage facility in New York.{a0_11} The project had about 550,000 Dth/d of firm capacity.{a0_11} In November 2012 the Commission approved a request to begin partial service on or before November 14. The company said it would seek approval for full service by December 1.{a0_11}
drafts.P8205:
Black Hills Energy said it was building the pipeline to improve reliability for its 57,000 customers in central Wyoming. The project included two new regulating stations, one in Casper and one in Glenrock. The company estimated the cost at $54.2 million.{a0_13}

The Energy Information Administration lists the line as completed in December 2019.{a0_8}
drafts.P8228:
A joint venture of TransCanada Corporation and Northwest Natural Gas Company filed its application with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in December 2008. The companies said that if the Commission approved the certificate by the end of 2009, construction could begin in 2010 with a target in-service date of November 2011.{a0_14}

Northwest Natural said the line would improve service reliability for its 655,000 customers and give access to more sources of gas. As proposed, it would also have connected to the proposed Bradwood Landing liquefied natural gas terminal in Clatsop County.{a0_14} The partners later withdrew the application, saying demand was not enough to support the project at that time. They said they planned to file a revised cross-Cascades proposal with Northwest Pipeline.{a0_15}
drafts.P8242:
Enterprise Products Partners and Duncan Energy Partners completed the Sherman Extension by March 2009. It expanded the Enterprise Texas Intrastate pipeline system through the Barnett Shale in north Texas. Throughput was about 360 MMcf/d at completion and was expected to reach about 950 MMcf/d in April 2009, as the rest of the 48,000 horsepower of compression came online.{a0_16} The partners said the extension added 1.1 Bcf/d of takeaway capacity from the region.{a0_16}

In December 2008 Enterprise announced a 40-mile supply lateral from the Trinity River Basin to the Sherman Extension near Justin, Texas. It was meant to carry Barnett Shale gas from Tarrant and Denton counties.{a0_17}
drafts.P8264:
In March 2010 staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission published an environmental assessment of the project under docket CP09-444. It covered 127.4 miles of 30-inch loop in seven segments in Pennsylvania and New Jersey. It also covered new compressor stations in Venango and McKean counties, Pennsylvania, and changes at seven existing compressor stations.{a0_18} The Commission approved the project, as reported in July 2010.{a0_19}

El Paso announced on November 1, 2011 that the project was in service. It added 350,000 Dth/d of capacity, all contracted to EQT Energy under a long-term agreement. The cost was about $0.7 billion.{a0_20}
drafts.P8265:
Commission staff published an environmental assessment of the project under docket CP11-161 in November 2011. It covered about 40.3 miles of 30-inch loop in five segments in Pennsylvania and New Jersey. It also covered changes at four existing compressor stations and a new meter station in Bergen County, New Jersey.{a0_21}

The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed in December 2013.{a0_8}
drafts.P8266:
In June 2000 Tennessee Gas Pipeline, a unit of El Paso Energy, announced the link. It said the link would give its customers access to the deepwater Gulf of Mexico and to other supply connected to the High Island Offshore System. Added supplies would flow to Vastar Resources' Grand Chenier, Louisiana, plant for processing.{a0_23}

Tennessee filed a request with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in docket CP00-441. A notice dated August 28, 2000 gave an estimated cost of $14,485,000.{a0_22} The notice gave a capability of 700 MMcf per day. Oil & Gas Journal reported 400 MMcfd.{a0_22}{a0_23} The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed in 2001.{a0_8}
drafts.P8094:
ANR applied to FERC in September 2002. The project would loop the Madison Lateral with 26.3 miles of 30-inch pipe in McHenry County, Illinois, and in Walworth and Rock Counties, Wisconsin. It would also replace 6.5 miles of 4-inch and 6-inch Beloit Lateral pipe with 20-inch pipe in Rock County. {b01fr02}{b01pow}{b01ogj1} The filing estimated 220,000 dekatherms per day of added capacity and a cost of $42.1 million. {b01pow}

ANR's 2004 annual report says the WestLeg facilities were completed. {b01anr} EIA lists the project as completed in October 2004. {b01eia}
drafts.P8107:
A FERC notice from December 2017 (docket PF17-7-000) said Cimarron River Pipeline LLC planned about 49.3 miles of new pipe in Beaver County, Oklahoma, and Seward County, Kansas. It also planned to lease 19.1 miles of an idle 26-inch pipeline. About 23 miles of the new pipe would be 20-inch and about 24.3 miles would be 30-inch, with short laterals to the National Helium Gas Processing Plant. The project would add up to 631 million standard cubic feet per day of firm capacity. {b01fr17}

EIA lists the project as an expansion sponsored by DCP Midstream, cancelled in July 2018 after the anchor shipper withdrew. {b01eia}
drafts.P8132:
The main line is 30-inch pipe that runs from Ewing Bank block 873 to the Larose processing plant in Louisiana. An Oil & Gas Journal article on its start-up called it the deepest 30-inch line in the Gulf at the time, with an ultimate capacity of 900 MMcf/d. {b01ogj2}

EIA lists the Discovery pipeline as completed in November 1997 under FERC docket CP96-712. It shows 147 miles of 18-inch, 24-inch and 30-inch pipe and a cost of $176.97 million. {b01eia} The Oil & Gas Journal article places the start-up in September 1998. {b01ogj2}
drafts.P8145:
FERC approved the lateral in February 2000 as a 60-mile line with a capacity of 130 MMcf/d. It would run from a new receipt point at Willcox, in Cochise County, toward the Mexican border, using 56 miles of 20-inch pipe. {b01ngiw}

EIA lists the project as completed on September 1, 2001, under FERC dockets CP99-322 and CP99-323. It shows 68 miles of 16-inch and 20-inch pipe. {b01eia}
drafts.P8316:
El Paso Natural Gas filed a prior notice with FERC on July 30, 2026 (docket CP26-558). The lateral would use 16-inch pipe and carry up to 167,000 dekatherms per day from the south mainline to a new McCloud Meter Station. The estimated cost was $20.3 million. The notice says only that the gas would go to a planned power generation facility. {b01fr26}

A Kinder Morgan open season posted in March 2026 offered the same 167,000 dekatherms per day, with Enchanted Rock as the receipt point and a target start of January 1, 2027. {b01os} Enchanted Rock is building the McCloud gas plant that El Paso Electric has proposed for Meta's data center in El Paso. {b01tt} An analyst post ties the open season to that plant. {b01mai} No regulator or company document names the lateral and the data center together.
drafts.P8167: Unitil's annual report for 2025 describes Granite State as an interstate gas transmission pipeline company with 85 miles of underground pipeline, mainly in Maine and New Hampshire. It serves Northern Utilities and is regulated by FERC. {b01uti}
drafts.P8318: EIA lists the three Abilene laterals as one project, Oracle Data Center Laterals (Hugh Brinson / North Texas). It is an intrastate Texas project with up to 900 MMcf/d of capacity. The first lateral entered service on June 13, 2026, and two more were targeted for mid-2026. EIA names the Oracle data center campus at Abilene as the customer. {b01eia}
drafts.P8193:
A FERC notice of May 6, 2025, describes the Magnum Gas Storage Project as two storage caverns with 21 billion cubic feet of working gas capacity, plus a 61.6-mile, 36-inch header pipeline. The header is already authorized under an earlier certificate. The April 2025 application asked FERC to amend that certificate again and to extend the construction deadline. {b01fr25}

EIA's May 2026 release lists the project as applied for, with 1,200 MMcf/d of added capacity and an in-service year of 2030. The August 2026 release no longer lists it. {b01eiaM}
drafts.P8206:
Natural Gas Pipeline Company of America announced the lateral in late 2000. It would extend the system into the East St. Louis market from Centralia, Illinois, using 24-inch pipe at an estimated cost of $35 million. Dynegy Marketing and Trade was the anchor customer. {b01ogj3} The project would add at least 300,000 dekatherms per day of capacity. {b01ngie} Completion was scheduled for June 2002.

EIA lists the project as completed in September 2002 at a cost of $37 million. {b01eia}
drafts.P8322:
Natural Gas Pipeline Company of America filed with FERC on September 17, 2026 (docket CP26-581). The project would rebuild Compressor Station 112 in Moore County, Texas, and add a delivery point in Deaf Smith County. {b01ngia}{b01mug}{b01gcm} It would add 321,200 dekatherms per day of southbound capacity on the Amarillo Line. With 228,800 dekatherms per day of existing unused space, the service would total 550,000 dekatherms per day. {b01ngia}{b01gcm} The filing estimated the cost at $139 million and an in-service date of September 1, 2028. {b01ngia}

The shipper, IP Roman III Gas, signed a 10-year precedent agreement on April 9 for the full 550,000 dekatherms per day. {b01ngia} Natural Gas Intelligence reports that IP Roman III Gas is an affiliate of Intersect Power, which Google acquired in March 2026. It says the gas would power the proposed Roman Energy Center, which would serve Google's Project Roman data center campus in Hereford, Texas. The filing does not name the end user. {b01ngia}
drafts.P8229:
Transcontinental Gas Pipe Line and Florida Gas Transmission developed the line jointly as the Pascagoula Expansion Project. FERC approved it as a connection between the two companies' existing systems and the new Gulf LNG import terminal near Pascagoula. The line would use 26-inch pipe, with 4.59 miles in Mobile County, Alabama, and 10.95 miles in Jackson County, Mississippi. It would cost $59 million and carry about 810,000 dekatherms per day. {b01pr}

EIA lists the project as completed in 2011. {b01eia}
drafts.P8243: EIA lists the Silo Pipeline Project as a lateral completed on June 23, 2016, under FERC docket CP15-26. It uses 6-inch pipe, adds 5 MMcf/d and cost $31.9 million. {b01eia}
drafts.P8267: EIA lists the Columbia Expansion as completed in November 1997 under FERC docket CP96-559. It used 24-inch and 36-inch pipe, added 142 MMcf/d and cost $63.1 million. {b01eia}
drafts.P8268: EIA lists Phase 1 of the TIME II Expansion as completed in November 2007 under FERC docket CP06-115. It used 36-inch pipe, added 150 MMcf/d and cost $116.7 million. EIA lists Pennsylvania, West Virginia and New Jersey as the states. {b01eia}
drafts.P8269: EIA lists the Transmission Incremental Market Expansion as completed in December 2002 under FERC docket CP02-32. It used 36-inch pipe, added 100 MMcf/d and cost $75.23 million. {b01eia}
drafts.P8311:
Williams Company was installing the pipeline, which would join the Rover Pipeline in southern Wood County, Ohio, and run through Henry, Liberty, Plain and Middleton townships to a power plant on Mercer Road.{a2_1} The plant sits just east of the Meta data center in Middleton Township, and Meta would be its only power customer.{a2_1}

At a Plain Township meeting in late July 2026, residents said they had not been told about the line. Williams representatives said they were under a tight timeline to get route details approved so construction could begin in September 2026.{a2_1}
drafts.P8108:
Energy Transfer Partners announced the line as a 42-inch pipe from Cleburne to Carthage, Texas. A Dallas Business Journal report from March 2006 said it would cost $535 million and carry 1.6 billion cubic feet a day.{a2_3} XTO Energy had signed to ship 200 million cubic feet a day for 10 years.{a2_3} Producers in the Fort Worth basin wanted an outlet to the Carthage hub, where gas sold for more than at western hubs.{a2_3}

Energy Transfer Partners later announced the Carthage Loop, a 32-mile loop of 42-inch pipe on the same line, to add 500 MMcf/d of capacity to Carthage.{a2_2} The company said construction was expected to begin in June 2008.{a2_2}
drafts.P8133: Dominion Cove Point LNG expanded its pipeline in Maryland with a 36-inch loop. The Energy Information Administration lists the project as adding 800 MMcf/d of capacity at a cost of $159.8 million.{a2_4}
drafts.P8134: The Energy Information Administration lists the Northeast TL-527 Line Project as a lateral that added 200 MMcf/d, built with 8-inch, 16-inch and 20-inch pipe under Federal Energy Regulatory Commission docket CP04-365.{a2_4}
drafts.P8168:
Paiute Pipeline Company applied to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to build the project in Elko County, Nevada. The company said it would provide 21,994 dekatherms a day of service.{a2_10} The Bureau of Land Management said the project would expand gas capacity to Elko for growing residential and business load and the energy needs of mining operations.{a2_9}

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued its certificate on May 14, 2015.{a2_9} In July 2015, the Bureau of Land Management signed a decision record approving a right-of-way for about 35.2 miles of new 8-inch pipe.{a2_9}
drafts.P8182:
Hutchinson Utilities Commission announced the pipeline in early 2003. A February 2003 report said the line would cost $26 million, with 16-inch pipe for 34 miles from Trimont to New Ulm and 12-inch pipe from New Ulm to Hutchinson.{a2_11} The commission awarded the construction contract to Jomax Construction Company, planned to begin site preparation on May 1, 2003, and expected completion in late summer 2003.{a2_11} It expected the line to supply 60,000 MMBtu a day.{a2_11}

The City of New Ulm says its gas reaches the city from the Northern Border Pipeline at Trimont over the Hutchinson pipeline.{a2_12}
drafts.P8194: Enbridge describes the system as a gathering pipeline of 14-inch to 24-inch pipe in the Gulf of Mexico, with a capacity of 800 MMcf/d.{a2_13} Enbridge operates it and holds a 74.33% interest.{a2_13}
drafts.P8207: Prospector Pipeline Company built the line to carry gas to the Barrick Goldstrike Mine, replacing propane as the fuel for the mine's gold ore processing.{a2_14} The line is a branch off the Ruby Pipeline. Q&D Construction installed the 12-inch steel pipe in under two months, and the project won an Engineering News-Record best project award in 2013.{a2_14}
drafts.P8230:
The Pennyrile Regional Energy Agency was created by the Todd County cities of Guthrie and Trenton.{a2_16} The agency first announced the pipeline in 2022 to bring a high-volume gas supply to Lyon, Caldwell, Trigg, Christian and Todd counties.{a2_15} The state budget gave the agency $30 million in 2022.{a2_16} The agency said Guthrie's gas supply from a small line from Clarksville, Tennessee, had run out, and it named large users such as a Novelis aluminum recycling plant in Guthrie.{a2_16}

In August 2024, the agency signed a letter of intent with Fort Campbell, and by January 2025 it had obtained 80% of the easements it needed.{a2_15} By March 2026 it was suing some landowners for easements. Whether the Kentucky Public Service Commission must approve the project was under dispute in Franklin Circuit Court.{a2_16} The agency had cited unforeseen delays in a 2025 lawsuit complaint, and the pipeline had not been built as of March 2026.{a2_16}
drafts.P8244:
Southern California Gas Company applied to the California Public Utilities Commission for the $621.3 million project, which also included a partial rebuild of the Adelanto Compressor Station.{a2_17} The company said the project would let the Honor Rancho storage field help support deliveries on the southern system.{a2_17}

On July 14, 2016, the commission denied the request. It found more cost-effective alternatives for supporting the southern system.{a2_17} It also said the company had not shown a need, because the line would not bring additional gas into Southern California.{a2_17}
drafts.P8270:
Texas Gas Transmission proposed this lateral together with the Greenville Lateral to move gas from the Fayetteville Shale in Arkansas to out-of-state markets.{a2_18} A Southwestern Energy subsidiary signed a precedent agreement in December 2006 as the foundation shipper.{a2_18} In February 2008, a report put the Fayetteville Lateral at about $502 million, within an $821 million project that included both laterals.{a2_18}

Federal Energy Regulatory Commission staff issued a draft environmental impact statement in November 2007.{a2_19} The company proposed two phases, the first 66 miles from Conway County to the Bald Knob area of White County, Arkansas, and the remaining 100 miles to Coahoma County, Mississippi.{a2_19} Southwestern Energy said in July 2009 that phase 1 went into service on December 24, 2008, and phase 2 on April 1, 2009.{a2_20}
drafts.P8271:
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's final environmental impact statement, noticed in March 2008, covered the 96.4-mile Greenville Lateral through Washington, Sunflower, Humphreys, Holmes and Attala counties, Mississippi.{a2_21} It also covered a 10,650-horsepower compressor station at Kosciusko.{a2_21} The lateral was permitted to carry about 768,000 MMBtu a day.{a2_21}

A February 2008 report put the lateral's cost at about $319 million.{a2_18} Southwestern Energy said in July 2009 that the Greenville Lateral went into service on April 1, 2009.{a2_20}
drafts.P8272:
Texas Gas Transmission proposed the project in 2021 to supply up to 220 million cubic feet a day to CenterPoint Energy's AB Brown Generating Station in Posey County, Indiana.{a2_22} The company said the project would support CenterPoint's retirement of four coal-fired units.{a2_22} The project also called for a new 4,863-horsepower compressor unit at the Slaughters Compressor Station in Webster County, Kentucky.{a2_22}

In July 2021, a local news report said the company had filed for federal approval.{a2_23} The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued its notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement on October 14, 2021, under docket CP21-467.{a2_22}
drafts.P8273: Texas Gas Transmission filed the project under Federal Energy Regulatory Commission docket CP15-14. A February 2015 Federal Register notice said it would add about 29.9 miles of 20-inch pipe and about 0.9 mile of 10-inch pipe.{a2_24} The notice said the project would serve two new industrial customers in Posey County, Indiana, with about 166,000 MMBtu a day of firm capacity.{a2_24}
drafts.P8274: The Energy Information Administration lists the West Greenville-Elkton Lateral as an expansion that added 80 MMcf/d and cost about $14.17 million.{a2_4}
drafts.P8275:
Texas Gas Transmission applied to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on March 4, 2015, for a 24-inch lateral to serve a new combined cycle generating unit at the Tennessee Valley Authority's Paradise plant.{a2_25} The lateral would provide a design capacity of up to 230,000 dekatherms a day.{a2_25} The company put the cost at $81 million.{a2_25}

A binding precedent agreement with the Tennessee Valley Authority covered the full design capacity for a primary term of 20 years.{a2_25} The company asked for an order by December 2015 so construction could begin in January 2016 and the line could be in service by September 2, 2016.{a2_26}
drafts.P8300: Wisconsin Gas, a subsidiary of Wisconsin Energy, announced the lateral on February 28, 2001. It began notifying officials and landowners in Ozaukee and Washington counties about route options for a proposed 16-mile line to serve the Port Washington Power Plant.{a2_27} The company planned to convert the plant from coal to natural gas as part of its Power the Future plan.{a2_27} It said it would submit route alternatives to the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin for review.{a2_27}
drafts.P8312:
Williams lists the Aristotle Central Pipeline among the Ohio siting cases of its Will-Power Pipeline OH affiliate. The cases are tied to the Socrates Power Solution Facilities, two proposed power plants of 200 megawatts each in New Albany, Ohio. Williams targeted service for Socrates South in the third quarter of 2026 and Socrates North in the fourth quarter of 2026.{a3_1}

The Ohio Power Siting Board listed an accelerated letter of notification for the Aristotle Central Pipeline Project, case 25-0847-GA-BLN, in its 2025 annual report.{a3_2}
drafts.P8109:
Cleopatra is a gas gathering line in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico. It is connected to the Holstein, Atlantis and Mad Dog platforms and brings gas to the market hub at Ship Shoal 332. Shell Midstream Partners said volumes moved under life-of-lease gathering agreements. The company said the line would also carry gas from Mad Dog 2.{a3_4}

Enbridge holds 22 percent. Shell Pipeline operates the line for the joint venture.{a3_3} Shell Midstream Partners bought a 1 percent interest from BP Pipelines on December 27, 2016.{a3_4} Enbridge gave the length as 110 miles in a fact sheet dated January 2025. Shell Midstream Partners gave it as 115 miles in its 2016 annual report.{a3_3}{a3_4}
drafts.P8147:
Empire Pipeline and National Fuel Gas Supply Corporation filed a joint application with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on March 18, 2014, under docket CP14-112. The filing covered about 17 miles of 12-inch and 16-inch pipeline in Steuben County, New York, and Tioga County, Pennsylvania. It also covered an interconnection with National Fuel's system, leased capacity, new firm and interruptible services, and additions at National Fuel's Tuscarora compressor station. The cost was about $43.7 million.{a3_8}

The U.S. Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed on November 4, 2015, adding 54 million cubic feet per day.{a3_7}
drafts.P8196:
MarkWest Pioneer submitted a pre-filing application to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in January 2008. The proposed line ran about 50 miles from MarkWest's gathering system in the Woodford Shale area to the proposed Midcontinent Express Pipeline interconnect at Bennington, Oklahoma. MarkWest signed agreements with Woodford producers, including Newfield Exploration, for more than 500 million cubic feet per day. It held an option to acquire 10 percent of Midcontinent Express equity after construction.{a3_16}

The U.S. Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed on July 14, 2009, under docket CP08-404. It gives a capacity of 638 million cubic feet per day and a cost of $75 million.{a3_7}
drafts.P8208:
Producers showed interest in late 2004 because existing carriers had limited capacity. Crosstex bought rights-of-way across Tarrant, Denton, Collin, Fannin, Delta and Lamar counties starting in early 2005. Construction began in October 2005 on two construction spreads with over 400 workers.{a3_17}{a3_18} Part of the system went into service in early February 2006 and the rest on April 4. Initial capacity was 250 million cubic feet per day, rising to 375 million with compression. The cost was $115 million.{a3_17}

EnLink Midstream later described the line as running about 140 miles from near Fort Worth to near Paris, Texas. It connects Barnett Shale production to markets reached through Natural Gas Pipeline Company of America, Kinder Morgan, Houston Pipeline, Atmos and Gulf Crossing. Throughput averaged about 338,000 million British thermal units per day from March 7 to December 31, 2014.{a3_19}
drafts.P8245: The U.S. Energy Information Administration lists the project as an expansion completed in February 2002. It lists the line as intrastate and regulated by the state.{a3_7}
drafts.P8329:
Wisconsin Electric Gas Operations, doing business as We Energies, applied to the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin in October 2024 under docket 6630-CG-139. It sought approval for a new 33-mile transmission line from its Bluff Creek liquefied natural gas facility to the Oak Creek and Elm Road Generating Station campus. The line would cross Kenosha, Racine and Milwaukee counties, with a Route A and a Route B. The estimated cost was $210.9 million for Route A and $217.1 million for Route B. The project also includes valve assemblies, a gate station and a regulator station. It would replace 2,287 feet of 16-inch line with 2,833 feet of 24-inch line.{a3_23}

The utility said it needed firm deliverability for the proposed Oak Creek Combustion Turbine and the Paris Reciprocating Internal Combustion Engine facility. It also planned to serve the Elm Road station once that station could run fully on gas. The commission issued an environmental assessment in May 2025 and a final decision on December 2, 2025. Construction was tentatively set to begin in late 2026, with completion by the end of 2027 in phases.{a3_23}
drafts.P8313:
Will-Power Pipeline OH, LLC filed a letter of notification with the Ohio Power Siting Board on June 23, 2025, asking for accelerated review.{a4_1} The line would supply the planned Socrates South power plant in New Albany. The board approved that 200 megawatt plant on June 9, 2025. The plant would serve an adjacent Meta-affiliated data center and run off the electric grid. The board said its gas would come from two 24-inch pipelines that would be the subject of later applications.{a4_2}

Williams lists Aristotle South with two other pipelines, Aristotle Central and Aristotle North, among the Socrates power facilities. Williams gave a target in-service date of the third quarter of 2026 for the Socrates South plant.{a4_3}
drafts.P8110:
Venture Global filed its application for the Plaquemines LNG Expansion with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) on November 17, 2025. The expansion would take feed gas from the Cloud Connector Pipeline, which was described as a new intrastate line in Louisiana that FERC does not regulate.{a4_4} The pipeline would carry gas from the Haynesville shale and connect with other intrastate pipelines.{a4_6}

An Arbo analysis from December 2025 said the pipeline would enter service in phases, with final completion projected for February 2029.{a4_4} On September 15, 2026, Baker Hughes announced it would supply 13 gas compression systems for the line.{a4_5}
drafts.P8136:
Double E Pipeline, LLC filed a prior notice request with FERC on June 11, 2026, under its blanket certificate. The filing was docketed as CP26-542. FERC published notice of the request in the Federal Register on June 25, 2026, with an estimated cost of $38 million and a protest deadline of August 21, 2026.{a4_7} Under the blanket rules, the work is allowed if no protest is filed in time, or if a protest is withdrawn within 30 days after the deadline.{a4_7}

The U.S. Energy Information Administration lists the lateral as serving a gas processing plant that Kinetik proposed near the new Dude meter station. It reports 330,000 dekatherms per day committed under two long-term agreements.{a4_8}
drafts.P8148:
FERC issued CenterPoint Energy Gas Transmission a certificate for the line on October 2, 2006. The certificate also covered two new compressor stations.{a4_9} The line was designed to carry up to 1.237 million dekatherms per day from Carthage in Panola County, Texas, to the Perryville Hub in Richland Parish, Louisiana.{a4_9}

FERC later raised the certificated capacity of the first two phases by about 36,000 dekatherms per day. It also approved a third phase to add compression, under docket CP07-41.{a4_9} The U.S. Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed, with a cost of $425 million.{a4_8}
drafts.P8149:
CenterPoint Energy Gas Transmission filed an application with FERC on January 26, 2005, under docket CP05-58. It sought to build about 21 miles of 24-inch pipeline and three more injection and withdrawal wells to enhance its Chiles Dome gas storage facility in Coal County, Oklahoma.{a4_10} It also asked to raise the maximum withdrawal rate to 309 million cubic feet per day.{a4_10}

A FERC staff notice of March 18, 2005, described about 23.4 miles of 24-inch pipeline for the Chiles Dome storage expansion, in Coal, Atoka, Pittsburg and Latimer counties.{a4_11}
drafts.P8150:
FERC staff started a pre-filing environmental review of the Tontitown Project in October 2007, under docket PF07-14. CenterPoint Energy Gas Transmission proposed about 16.0 miles of 24-inch pipeline, called the OM-1-A pipeline, next to an existing interstate pipeline in Logan and Franklin counties, Arkansas.{a4_12} The project also included a 10,310-horsepower compressor station in Le Flore County, Oklahoma.{a4_12}

The U.S. Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed in January 2009, under FERC docket CP08-69.{a4_8}
drafts.P8171:
Guardian Pipeline, L.L.C. filed an application with FERC on July 1, 2026, under docket CP26-548, for its Guardian 3 Expansion Project in Illinois and Wisconsin.{a4_13} The project would add two 36-inch loops. The Joliet Loop would run about 42.6 miles in Kendall and DeKalb counties. The Sycamore Loop would run about 25.5 miles in DeKalb and McHenry counties.{a4_13} It would also add compression in Illinois, a new compressor station in Dodge County, Wisconsin, and a new meter station in Fond du Lac County, Wisconsin.{a4_13}

Guardian said the project was fully subscribed under binding precedent agreements.{a4_13} After two binding open seasons in 2025, it secured commitments from five local utilities for all of the capacity.{a4_14} Guardian requested a certificate by June 2027. It proposed to start construction in September 2027 and to be in service in November 2028.{a4_14}
drafts.P8319: Joule Capital Partners applied to Millard County, Utah, for a legislative development agreement to allow a 24-inch natural gas transmission pipeline that the zoning does not otherwise permit. The route would run mostly across private land. The county planning commission scheduled a public hearing for May 7, 2026, and would forward a recommendation to the county commissioners.{a4_15}
drafts.P8197:
Energy Transfer announced in 2008 that it had completed the Maypearl-to-Malone line, along with the Paris Loop pipeline. The company said the 36-inch line added 600 MCFD of capacity out of the Barnett Shale.{a4_16}

The U.S. Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed in August 2008. It describes it as an intrastate line regulated by the state, with no FERC docket.{a4_8}
drafts.P8232: Piedmont Natural Gas completed the Sutton Pipeline Project to supply the 625 megawatt Sutton combined-cycle plant in North Carolina. The project included 120 miles of 20-inch pipeline and 8 miles of 30-inch pipeline. It also added about 25,000 horsepower of compression on Piedmont's system.{a4_17} The plant was expected to begin commercial operation in late 2013, and Duke Energy said it would retire 575 megawatts of coal-fired units at the site by then.{a4_17}
drafts.P8324:
Energy Transfer and Entergy Louisiana announced a 20-year firm transportation agreement in November 2025. It called for 250,000 MMBtu per day of firm service from February 2028 through January 2048, with an option for Entergy to expand capacity.{a4_18} The gas would supply Entergy Louisiana's planned combined-cycle plants and Meta's hyperscale data center in Richland Parish, Louisiana.{a4_18} Energy Transfer said it would build the 12-mile lateral off the Tiger Pipeline to meet the agreement.{a4_18}

The U.S. Energy Information Administration ties the lateral to Entergy Louisiana's planned Titanium Advanced Power Station in Richland Parish.{a4_8}
drafts.P8301: The U.S. Energy Information Administration lists the Wild Goose Lateral as an intrastate lateral built by Wild Goose Storage and completed on November 20, 2003. It reports 30-inch pipe and a cost of $20 million.{a4_8}
drafts.P8095:
Atmos Energy and Energy Transfer Partners announced a letter of intent in January 2005 to build, own and operate the line together. They called it the North Side Loop.{a5_1} The companies described an initial capacity of 200,000 MMBtu/d, with room to expand to 500,000 MMBtu/d later.{a5_1} Energy Transfer would provide the initial capital, and Atmos would contribute its share within two years of signing a definitive agreement.{a5_1}

The Energy Information Administration (EIA) lists the line as two halves. The West Side was completed in May 2005 and the East Side in October 2006.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8111:
Colorado Interstate Gas filed the Front Range Expansion with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) on October 2, 2000, under docket CP01-1.{a5_8} A FERC environmental notice in November 2000 described the Fort Morgan Storage Field Expansion Project, which included two 24-inch pipeline loops, one of 26.2 miles and one of 27 miles, along with a new compressor station at Fort Lupton.{a5_2} FERC issued its certificate on May 16, 2001.{a5_3}

The EIA lists the project as completed in October 2001, at a cost of $58 million.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8112:
Colorado Interstate Gas filed its application with FERC on September 10, 2009, under docket CP09-464.{a5_4} The filing called the project the North Raton Lateral, also known as the Raton 2010 Expansion Project.{a5_4} The line would be about 118.6 miles of 16-inch pipe, with about 130,000 Dth/d of capacity subject to long-term firm transportation agreements.{a5_4} The company put the cost at about $132 million.{a5_4}

The EIA lists the project as completed on November 18, 2010.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8113:
Colorado Interstate Gas applied to FERC under docket CP02-6 for facilities to move more gas out of the Raton Basin. The first proposal was for about 57.8 MMcf/d, using loops on the Campo Lateral and on Line 3A.{a5_5} On March 4, 2002, the company amended the application and shortened the loops.{a5_5} One shipper could not meet the terms of its precedent agreement, and that agreement ended.{a5_5} The revised loops were 22.10 miles and 24.20 miles of 16-inch pipe on the Campo Lateral and 7.67 miles of 20-inch pipe on Line 3A, at an estimated cost of $22,070,400.{a5_5}

The EIA lists the project as completed on December 15, 2002.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8114:
FERC issued a certificate for the project in May 2005 under docket CP05-50.{a5_6} The expansion also included 1,775 horsepower of added compression at the Beaver Compressor Station in Oklahoma, at a total cost of $61 million.{a5_6} Five producers signed firm transportation agreements with minimum terms of 10 years: Pioneer Natural Resources, El Paso Energy Raton, Red River Ranch Holding, Apple Tree Holdings and XTO Energy.{a5_6}

The EIA lists the project as completed in December 2005.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8115:
Colorado Interstate Gas filed an application with FERC on September 5, 2000, under docket CP00-452. The project was meant to add 85 MDth per day of capacity out of the Raton Basin.{a5_7} It also included a new compressor unit at the Keyes Compressor Station.{a5_7} The company put the cost of the expansion at $51,784,900.{a5_7}

The EIA lists the project as completed in October 2001.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8116:
A FERC environmental notice dated February 6, 2001 described the project under docket CP01-45. It said the expansion would let Colorado Interstate Gas carry an additional 278.8 MMcf/d between the Cheyenne Hub and the Watkins Compressor Station, and 344.4 MMcf/d on the part of the Valley Line that the new pipe would parallel.{a5_8} The notice listed two pipe sections. One was about 35.1 miles of 24-inch loop from the Ault Meter Station to a new Fort Lupton Compressor Station. The other was about 84 miles of 20-inch pipe running roughly parallel to the existing Valley Line from the Watkins Compressor Station to the Nixon Power Plant.{a5_8} The Fort Lupton station would hold 4,450 horsepower of compression.{a5_8}

The EIA lists the project as completed in December 2002, at a cost of $72.14 million.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8172: The EIA lists the lateral as completed on May 30, 2014, at a cost of $26.3 million. The EIA record gives FERC docket CP13-64.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8184:
Kern River proposed the Apex Expansion in November 2009.{a5_9} FERC issued its final environmental impact statement on July 23, 2010, under docket CP10-14.{a5_10} FERC approved the project in September 2010, and construction began in October 2010.{a5_9} The Wasatch Loop was built through the Wasatch Mountains in Morgan, Davis and Salt Lake counties. The loop was meant to relieve a bottleneck.{a5_9}

The project also included a new compressor station at Milford in Beaver County, Utah, and added compression at the Coyote Creek, Elberta and Dry Lake stations.{a5_9} The project cost about $373 million, and the line entered service in October 2011.{a5_9}
drafts.P8185:
Kern River filed an application with FERC on July 18, 2001, under docket CP01-405.{a5_11} The lateral would serve the High Desert Power Project, a gas-fired combined-cycle plant being built near Victorville.{a5_11} Victorville-Gas, the plant's fuel supplier, signed a binding precedent agreement for the full 282,000 Dth per day of design capacity, for a primary term of 21 years.{a5_11} Test operations at the plant were scheduled for September 2002.{a5_11}

The EIA lists the lateral as completed in September 2002, at a cost of $29 million.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8310: Kern River filed an application with FERC on March 15, 2001, under docket CP01-106. It asked for temporary and permanent certificates for emergency facilities that would add up to 135,000 Mcf per day of limited-term capacity from Wyoming to California, to help meet an urgent need for power in California.{a5_12} The facilities were three new compressor stations at Elberta and Veyo in Utah and Daggett in California.{a5_12} Kern River expected them to be in service about July 1, 2001, at a cost of about $81 million.{a5_12} The company said that after the California emergency the remaining temporary facilities would become part of its 2002 or 2003 expansion projects.{a5_12}
drafts.P8198: MichCon announced the project in April 2007. The company said it would increase gas supplies in West Michigan, meet growth in demand, and improve the reliability of supply to the southern Grand Rapids area.{a5_13} MichCon said construction would begin in June and finish in the 2008 construction season.{a5_13} About 92 percent of the line would sit in an electrical transmission tower right-of-way.{a5_13} The project also included a meter and odorization station in Hudsonville, a pressure-reduction station in Byron Township and two more connections to the MichCon distribution system.{a5_13} MichCon had filed its application with the Michigan Public Service Commission on January 16. The estimated cost was $70 million.{a5_13}
drafts.P8209: The lateral was built to carry regasified natural gas from the Northeast Gateway deepwater liquefied natural gas port. The port was developed by Excelerate Energy.{a5_15} FERC issued Algonquin a certificate in March 2007.{a5_15} The line could deliver up to 800,000 Dth/d, and the company targeted operation for the 2007-2008 winter.{a5_15} Algonquin let a pipelay contract in March 2007 to Horizon Offshore Contractors. The work also covered two 18-inch laterals, and it was expected to run from May to November.{a5_16} FERC cleared Algonquin to begin construction in May 2007, after the port received its federal license.{a5_14}
drafts.P8233:
Piedmont Natural Gas reached an agreement in October 2009 with Progress Energy Carolinas to deliver gas to a power plant to be built at its Wayne County, North Carolina, site. The North Carolina Utilities Commission approved the agreement in May 2010.{a5_18} The plan called for about 38 miles of 20-inch pipe plus compression, with service to the plant by June 2012.{a5_18} Piedmont also agreed with Cardinal Pipeline Company to add 149,000 dekatherms per day to its firm capacity there. Cardinal would spend an estimated $48 million to expand, and Piedmont held a 21.49 percent stake in Cardinal.{a5_18}

The plant was part of Progress Energy's plan to replace coal-fired generating plants with gas-fired ones.{a5_19} The EIA lists the pipeline as completed in June 2012.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8277:
The pipeline was proposed to supply gas to the Union Power Partners power plant in Union County, Arkansas. A FERC environmental notice from February 2000, under docket CP00-47, said the line would deliver 430,000 decatherms per day to the plant.{a5_20} The notice also listed two mainline valves.{a5_20}

The EIA lists the project as completed on October 30, 2001, at a cost of $45 million.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8302: The EIA project note said the line would improve supply and reliability for local distribution and agriculture customers by giving access to producing basins through WBI's existing system.{a5_eia}
drafts.P8097:
Bay Gas Storage Company, a unit of EnergySouth, built the line to connect its storage site to Gulf South's 30-inch pipeline near Whistler, Alabama.{a6_1} It was developed to meet the requirements of the Barry power plant, which Gulf South serves for Alabama Power. The company's president also described it as part of a strategy to build a storage hub around Mobile Bay.{a6_1}

Oil & Gas Journal reported the line complete in December 2001. The Energy Information Administration lists the completion date as July 22, 2001.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8117:
Kinder Morgan Interstate Gas Transmission proposed the Colorado Lateral Expansion Project under FERC docket CP07-430. A FERC environmental assessment notice in January 2008 described 41.4 miles of 12-inch pipe in Weld County, Colorado, plus five lateral distribution lines totaling 10.8 miles.{a6_2} The stated purpose was to add 57 MMcf/d of capacity from the Cheyenne Hub to the Greeley area.{a6_2}

The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed in December 2008, at 74 MMcf/d.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8156: Energy Transfer Company built the line as a new intrastate pipeline. The Energy Information Administration lists it as completed on December 15, 2006, at 400 MMcf/d and a cost of 48 million dollars.{a6_eia} The agency spells the name "ET Mayprearl to Mansfield Line."{a6_eia}
drafts.P8173:
Gulf South filed notice on April 14, 2006 to build the loop under its blanket certificate, in docket CP06-127. The loop runs next to the existing 24-inch Index 266 line and includes a new meter station at Carthage Junction.{a6_4} Gulf South said East Texas production growth had strained takeaway capacity. Its firm capacity from East Texas was sold out through 2009, and customers were asking for more.{a6_4}

The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed on December 15, 2006, at 122.4 MMcf/d.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8174:
Gulf South, a Boardwalk Pipelines subsidiary, announced a binding open season in October 2025 after a foundation shipper signed a precedent agreement.{a6_5} The project would gather gas from the Katy and Carthage hubs and deliver it near Gillis in southwest Louisiana, serving LNG exporters, utilities and industrial users. It also includes upgrades on the Index 129 line and a new compressor station near Cleveland, Texas.{a6_5} Boardwalk targeted service by November 1, 2029.{a6_5}{a6_6}

The Energy Information Administration lists FERC docket CP26-547, with the application filed June 26, 2026.{a6_eia} Oil & Gas Journal reported that the project was accepted into the federal FAST-41 permitting program and put the cost at 1.4 billion dollars.{a6_7}
drafts.P8186:
Kinder Morgan Louisiana Pipeline is a subsidiary of Kinder Morgan Energy Partners. It was proposed to carry regasified LNG from Cheniere's Sabine Pass import terminal, then under construction in Cameron Parish, Louisiana.{a6_8} FERC approved the application in June 2007. The first leg is 132 miles of 42-inch pipe to a Columbia Gulf interconnect in Evangeline Parish, with a 2.3-mile, 24-inch lateral to a Florida Gas Transmission compressor station in Acadia Parish. The second leg is one mile of 36-inch pipe to the Natural Gas Pipeline Company of America. The line connects with many interstate pipelines.{a6_8} The estimated cost at approval was 517 million dollars.{a6_8}

The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed on June 21, 2009, at 2,130 MMcf/d and a cost of 1,000 million dollars.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8199:
Consumers Energy filed its application on August 23, 2019. The Michigan Public Service Commission approved it on November 19, 2020, in Case U-20618.{a6_9} The new 36-inch line replaces Line 100A, a 20-inch pipeline built in 1949. The company cited corrosion, seam weld and other anomalies, and a gas-supply bottleneck in the smaller pipe. It also rerouted portions to avoid densely populated areas.{a6_10}

At approval, construction was expected in 2023 and 2024 at an estimated cost of 550 million dollars.{a6_10} Consumers Energy said on November 4, 2024 that it had finished the replacement across Clinton, Shiawassee, Ingham, Livingston and Washtenaw counties.{a6_11}
drafts.P8210:
Northern Natural Gas filed its application on April 17, 2026, in FERC docket CP26-241. The project also includes a 9.03-mile, 20-inch loop of the Omaha 3rd branch line, a 2.48-mile, 20-inch extension of the Des Moines C-line, a 9.83-mile uprate, and a new 20,500 horsepower compressor station.{a6_12} It would provide 535,360 dekatherms per day of incremental firm service. The notice says the service is fully subscribed. The cost is about 187.5 million dollars.{a6_12}

The Energy Information Administration lists Nebraska Public Power District as the anchor shipper at 445,000 Dth/d. The gas would serve the district's 694-megawatt Princeton Road power plant. Northern asked for FERC approval by March 2027.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8211: The Energy Information Administration lists the project as an expansion completed in November 1997, under FERC docket CP97-27. It added 244 MMcf/d at a cost of 102 million dollars and served Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, Minnesota and Wisconsin.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8212:
Northern Natural Gas filed its application on May 28, 2026, in FERC docket CP26-534. The project would provide about 361,600 dekatherms per day to a new gas-fired power plant in Gaines County, Texas. FERC planned to issue its environmental assessment on February 19, 2027, with a federal authorization deadline of May 20, 2027.{a6_13}

The project includes 15.1 miles of 24-inch pipe in Lea County, New Mexico, and 1.1 miles of 16-inch pipe in Gaines County, Texas. It adds a 7,700 horsepower compressor station and an interconnect with Transwestern at the Phillips 66 Linam Ranch plant. A delivery point would serve Southwestern Public Service Company's planned Gaines County Generating Station. Pipeline & Gas Journal reported a capacity of 361 MMcf/d and a cost of 104.9 million dollars.{a6_14}
drafts.P8213: The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed on November 1, 1996, under FERC docket CP96-57. It added 46.4 MMcf/d of capacity at a cost of 18.5 million dollars.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8330:
Palo Duro Transmission, working with Producers Midstream, held a binding open season from June 30 to July 14, 2025. Producers Midstream said the project would link Waha residue gas markets in the Permian Basin with Mid-Continent markets in the Anadarko Basin. It targeted industrial, petrochemical, power generation and AI-related behind-the-meter demand.{a6_16} East Daley Analytics said it would serve data centers, petrochemical plants and power generators. It said that if fully dedicated to data centers, the line could support 125 to 150 megawatts of load. No new construction is needed, and it connects to Northern Natural, Southern Star, ANR, NGPL, Panhandle Eastern, Enable and Transwestern.{a6_17}

Palo Duro Transmission signed a binding precedent agreement with Scurry Downstream, an affiliate of Producers Midstream, for all of the capacity. It filed its application on August 1, 2025 and amended it on December 22, 2025. No comments or protests were filed.{a6_15} The project lets Palo Duro Transmission operate the northern 61 miles of the existing pipeline as an interstate line and lease 80,000 Dth/d of capacity on the header pipeline. FERC issued the certificates on March 19, 2026.{a6_15}
drafts.P8248: Northwest Natural Gas built the lateral as an intrastate line. The Energy Information Administration lists it as completed on November 1, 1999, at 190 MMcf/d and a cost of 35 million dollars.{a6_eia} The agency lists later phases of the South Mist storage link as separate projects.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8280: The Energy Information Administration lists the project as an expansion completed in June 2002, under FERC docket CP01-389. It added 126 MMcf/d at a cost of 128 million dollars.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8281:
Transco proposed the project under FERC docket CP13-551. A FERC environmental assessment in August 2014 described four 42-inch loops totaling 29.8 miles in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, plus added compression at four existing compressor stations. Transco said the project would provide 525,000 dekatherms per day of firm capacity to the mid-Atlantic and Southeast. It said it had binding agreements with shippers for the entire capacity.{a6_23}

The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed on January 5, 2016, at a cost of 610 million dollars.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8282: The Energy Information Administration lists the project as an expansion completed in December 1997, under FERC docket CP97-193. It added 38 MMcf/d in North Carolina at a cost of 13.2 million dollars.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8283: The Energy Information Administration lists the first phase of the Mid-South Expansion, under FERC docket CP11-18, as completed on May 15, 2012. It added 95 MMcf/d at a cost of 92.5 million dollars.{a6_eia} The agency lists the second phase as a separate project completed in June 2013.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8284:
A FERC environmental assessment notice in December 1997 described the project under docket CP97-92. It covered 19.08 miles of 30-inch pipe from Compressor Station 82 in Mobile County, Alabama, to a new offshore platform, and 56.58 miles of 24-inch pipe from there to a platform in Main Pass Viosca Knoll Block 261. It also added 15,000 horsepower of compression at Station 82 and 15,000 horsepower at a new Station 83. The stated purpose was to provide about 350,000 Mcf/d on the offshore facilities.{a6_24}

The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed in August 1998, at a cost of 120.2 million dollars.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8285:
Transco proposed the Momentum Expansion in docket CP01-388. In September 2001 it amended its application, eliminating some loops and compression and shortening other loops. The shortened loops stay essentially within the footprint of those originally proposed.{a6_25}

The Energy Information Administration lists the first phase as completed in May 2003, at 262 MMcf/d and a cost of 163.85 million dollars.{a6_eia} It lists the second phase as a separate project completed in February 2004.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8286: The Energy Information Administration lists the Potomac Expansion, under FERC docket CP06-421, as completed on November 9, 2007. It added 165 MMcf/d at a cost of 76.4 million dollars.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8287:
Transco and the South Carolina Public Service Authority, known as Santee Cooper, proposed the SouthCoast Expansion in 1999. A FERC notice in November 1999 described about 44.3 miles of pipeline and 31,500 horsepower of compression in Alabama and Georgia. Santee Cooper would have built about 5 miles of 16-inch pipe to its planned power plant.{a6_26}

The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed on November 3, 2000, at 200 MMcf/d and a cost of 108 million dollars.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8288:
Transco filed its application for the Sundance Expansion on April 3, 2000. The project was to add about 228 MMcf/d of firm capacity from Transco's Station 65 in Louisiana to delivery points in Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina. FERC authorized it on March 29, 2001, and Transco accepted the order on April 6, 2001. The project called for about 38 miles of new loop and about 33,000 horsepower of new compression, with a target in-service date of May 2002 and an estimated cost of about 134 million dollars.{a6_27}

The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed in May 2002, at 230 MMcf/d.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8289:
A September 2012 FERC notice for docket CP13-30 described about 91.4 miles of new 24-inch pipe next to the existing South Virginia Lateral and 7.2 miles of new 24-inch pipe in Brunswick County, Virginia. It also included a compressor station in Pittsylvania County.{a6_29} Pipeline & Gas Journal reported in September 2015 that Williams had placed the expansion in service to fuel new electric power generation in North Carolina. The expansion provides 270,000 dekatherms per day and cost 300 million dollars.{a6_28}

The Energy Information Administration lists the project as completed on August 27, 2015.{a6_eia}
drafts.P8303:
The Public Service Commission of Wisconsin voted on June 5, 2001 to approve the lateral. It connects Wisconsin Gas' existing facilities to the Guardian Pipeline near Ixonia in Jefferson County, bringing gas from the Chicago market hub to southeastern Wisconsin. The company said it would introduce pipeline competition in the region. The commission chose the company's recommended route, which was 78 percent co-located with the Union Pacific Railroad and other existing utility infrastructure.{a6_30} Construction was scheduled to begin in spring 2002, with commercial operation in the fall of that year.{a6_30}

The lateral serves We Energies distribution facilities in Brookfield and Germantown. Planning and construction took four years. Gulf Interstate Engineering was the design engineer.{a6_31}
drafts.P8098:
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued a certificate in December 2006 to Equitrans, a subsidiary of Equitable Resources. The line would give Kentucky producers 130 MDth/d of takeaway capacity. An in-service date of April 1, 2007 was anticipated. {a7_1}

EQT sold the line to Spectra Energy Partners for $390 million in 2011. The sale announcement said the line was placed in service in April 2008. {a7_2}
drafts.P8118:
The project added about 19.1 miles of 20-inch and 26-inch loop plus aboveground facilities in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, New York and Maryland. It was designed to provide 312,000 Dth/d of firm service to growing mid-Atlantic markets. {a7_3}

The project was completed in October 2015 at a reported cost of $269 million. {a7_eia}
drafts.P8121: The project was completed on October 28, 2014 at a reported cost of $132 million. {a7_eia}
drafts.P8123:
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approved the project, according to a TC Energy statement of November 17, 2023. About 48 miles of 1950s 12-inch pipe would be replaced with 24-inch pipe. Construction was expected to begin by the second quarter of 2024, with service projected for November 1, 2025. {a7_8}

TC Energy began construction in July 2024. Local environmental groups opposed the project. {a7_9}
drafts.P8153:
Enterprise Products announced on June 29, 2010 a 350-mile expansion of its system for the Eagle Ford shale. It included a cryogenic processing facility, a natural gas liquids line to Mont Belvieu and a residue gas line to the Wilson storage facility in Wharton County, Texas. Wilson connects to the Trunkline, Tennessee Gas, Transco, NGPL and Gulf South systems. {a7_11}

Enterprise completed the 36-inch residue gas pipeline in April 2012. {a7_10}
drafts.P8175:
Gulfstream filed Phase IV with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in January 2007 and awarded the engineering contract to Willbros. The expansion carried an estimated cost of $117 million and included 45,000 hp of new compression. {a7_12}

It was built to serve a repowering of the Bartow power plant in St. Petersburg, Florida. {a7_12}
drafts.P8187:
FPL Energy announced on October 2, 2001 that it would work with TXU and Kinder Morgan to supply gas to a new power plant. Kinder Morgan North Texas Pipeline would build an 85-mile 30-inch line from an interconnect in Lamar County to the 1,789 MW Forney plant in Kaufman County, Texas. The line would also serve the existing 1,000 MW Paris plant. {a7_13}

Construction was to begin the following summer, and the Forney plant was expected to be operating in mid-2003. {a7_13}
drafts.P8200:
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission staff issued an environmental assessment in October 2005. The line would start at the Portland Station in Sumner County, Tennessee. It would deliver up to 120,000 Dth/d to Piedmont Natural Gas Company, a local distribution company, under long-term transportation service. {a7_14}

The project was completed on April 15, 2008 at a reported cost of $26.27 million. {a7_eia}
drafts.P8215:
Northwest proposed the lateral in 2007 to move Piceance Basin gas from the White River Hub near Meeker to its mainline. It estimated a cost of up to $53 million and service as early as November 2009. The project could also help re-contract 200 MMcf/d of capacity from Stanfield, Oregon to Ignacio, Colorado held by Pan-Alberta Gas. {a7_17}

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued a certificate in April 2009 for the 24-inch, 27.4-mile pipeline. It provides about 360,000 Dth/d of firm service to Ignacio, where Northwest interconnects with El Paso Natural Gas and Transwestern. Construction was expected in May 2009, with service by November 1, 2009. {a7_18}
drafts.P8217: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission staff issued an environmental assessment in March 2002. The pipeline would run from Northwest's existing system near Ranier in Thurston County, Washington to the Satsop Combustion Turbine Project in Grays Harbor County. The project also included added compression at the Tumwater Compressor Station. {a7_19}

BP and Shell Gas Transmission announced the project on May 17, 2001 as a $150 million, 100-mile gathering line for the ultradeepwater Gulf of Mexico. It would connect ultradeepwater developments with the Destin Pipeline, which lands in Mississippi.{b12_11} BP would operate Okeanos Gas Gathering Company with two-thirds ownership. Shell would hold the rest.{b12_11}

The line was planned in two phases beginning in 2002. The first was a 74-mile, 24-inch segment to gather gas from the Na Kika project, due for the 2003 start-up. The second was a 26-mile segment to connect the Crazy Horse field, due in 2005.{b12_11} Enbridge's offshore pipelines page lists Okeanos among its natural gas systems.{b12_12}
drafts.P8239:
Progress Energy said on March 5, 2001 that its subsidiary North Carolina Natural Gas had finished building the line. Construction began in the fall of 2000 and took about five months. About 73 miles of the route ran along an existing company corridor, with new right of way in Anson and Richmond counties.{b12_13}

The pipeline was built to supply a 620-megawatt Carolina Power & Light plant in Richmond County, which was due to start in June 2001. It would first carry 200 to 300 million cubic feet per day. Adding compression could raise that to 800 million.{b12_13}
drafts.P8261:
Targa announced Bull Run II on August 18, 2026, together with new 20-year agreements with ExxonMobil. The line would be added to Targa's existing Bull Run residue gas system. It would carry gas from three planned Delaware basin processing plants, Wrangler, Ranger and Ranger II.{b12_14}{b12_15}

The plants would total about 825 million cubic feet per day. Take-or-pay commitments would back the pipeline. Targa said it expected operations to begin in the first half of 2028.{b12_14}{b12_15}
drafts.P8296:
Pecan Pipeline Company, a wholly owned subsidiary of EOG Resources, had a permit approved in July 2022 for a 41-mile line in Webb and Duval counties. The line supports EOG's Dorado gas field in the Austin Chalk of Webb County.{b12_16}

The U.S. Energy Information Administration says the first phase was completed in 2023 and the second in the second half of 2024. The line would connect with other pipelines at the Agua Dulce hub area.{b12_5}
drafts.P8105:
Cardinal Pipeline Company, LLC announced in March 2010 that it had signed precedent agreements to add 199,000 dekatherms per day of firm transportation capacity. The $39 million Cardinal System Expansion was scheduled to enter service in July 2012. It was designed to serve growth on the Piedmont Natural Gas and PSNC Energy systems, including a gas-fired power plant that Progress Energy Carolinas planned in Wayne County.{b13_1}

The pipeline company is a North Carolina limited liability company. Its members are wholly owned subsidiaries of Williams Partners, PSNC Energy and Piedmont. The line receives gas at an interconnect with the Transco pipeline.{b13_1}
drafts.P8130:
Midcoast Energy Resources agreed in July 2000 to move up to 276 million cubic feet per day of gas for Calpine Corporation. The gas was for two Calpine power plants near Decatur, Alabama, the 700 megawatt Decatur Energy Center and the 660 megawatt Morgan Energy Center. The agreement ran for 20 years, and deliveries were expected to begin by summer 2002.{b13_2}

Midcoast said it would build a 52 mile pipeline near its existing Midcoast Interstate Transmission system.{b13_2}
drafts.P8140:
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) staff issued an environmental assessment of the proposed Jewell Ridge Lateral in December 2005, under docket CP05-413.{b13_3}

East Tennessee Natural Gas, then a unit of Duke Energy Gas Transmission, placed the lateral in service in November 2006. It runs from a compressor station northwest of Richlands, Virginia, and links the western Virginia operations of CNX Gas to the East Tennessee mainline near Marion in Smyth County. It also connects with the Transco pipeline at Cascade Creek, North Carolina. CNX Gas signed a 15-year agreement for 210 million cubic feet per day of firm transportation.{b13_4}
drafts.P8141:
East Tennessee Natural Gas Company filed an application with FERC on February 2, 2001, under docket CP01-80-000. It asked to build the Murray Lateral as an extension of its Line 3500, together with four pipeline loops in Tennessee. The estimated cost was $69,390,000.{b13_5}

The line was to serve Dalton Utilities and the City of Cartersville, Georgia, with 5,000 dekatherms per day. It was also to deliver up to 165,000 dekatherms per day to Duke Energy Murray, LLC, for a 1,240 megawatt gas-fired power plant in Murray County, Georgia. East Tennessee asked FERC for a certificate by August 15, 2001.{b13_5}
drafts.P8142:
East Tennessee Natural Gas, LLC filed a FERC application on March 8, 2010, under docket CP10-89. The filing covered an 8.4 mile mainline extension and 8.0 miles of pipeline looping. It also covered replacing 11.5 miles of older 8 inch and 12 inch pipe with 24 inch pipe. The project would give 150,000 dekatherms per day of firm service to a proposed Tennessee Valley Authority gas-fired power plant. FERC staff had opened pre-filing review in August 2009.{b13_6}

In July 2010, FERC staff issued an environmental assessment. It said the plant was the John Sevier Combined Cycle Plant and concluded that approval would not be a major federal action significantly affecting the environment.{b13_7}
drafts.P8165:
Gas Transmission Northwest, LLC filed an application with FERC on July 31, 2012, under docket CP12-494. The lateral was meant to serve the Carty Generating Station that Portland General Electric Company proposed in Morrow County, Oregon. FERC had accepted the project into its pre-filing process on March 31, 2011.{b13_12}

FERC's list of approved projects shows the certificate issued on March 14, 2013, for 175 million cubic feet per day.{b13_13}
drafts.P8317:
Homer City Generation, L.P. applied to the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection for permit PAD320011 to build the pipeline. The line would run from a metering and interconnect facility in Burrell Township to the Homer City Generating Station in Center Township, Indiana County.{b13_14} The department took public comment on the permit through March 9, 2026, and held a public hearing in Indiana, Pennsylvania, in May 2026. Reports described the line as designed to feed the redeveloped plant and the data center campus beside it.{b13_15}{b13_16}

Homer City Redevelopment announced in April 2025 a 4.5 gigawatt gas-fired power plant and data centers on a 3,200 acre site. The project was put at $10 billion. Construction began in April 2026, and the plant was expected to produce power in 2028.{b13_16} A September 2026 trade report described a proposed Amazon Web Services campus of up to 39 data center buildings at the site.{b13_18}
drafts.P8227:
Oregon LNG proposed the pipeline as a connector to its bidirectional liquefied natural gas terminal at Warrenton, Oregon. In August 2015, FERC issued a draft environmental impact statement covering the terminal, the pipeline and an upgrade of part of the Northwest Pipeline in Washington. Comments were due by October 6, 2015, and FERC had set February 12, 2016, for the final statement.{b13_19}{b13_20}

Oregon LNG withdrew the project in April 2016. A company representative told the Warrenton mayor that Leucadia National Corporation, the holding company behind the project, was no longer willing to fund it.{b13_21}{b13_22}
drafts.P8240:
FERC approved a purchase in April 2006, under docket CP06-57, in which El Paso Natural Gas would buy a 37 mile lateral from the Salt River Project Agricultural Improvement and Power District for about $32 million. The lateral had a capacity of 342,500 dekatherms per day and connected El Paso's South System Line 2000 to the Santan power plant in Gilbert, Arizona.{b13_23}

El Paso said it planned to connect the northern end to its Line 2222 and reverse the flow on that line toward Phoenix. The purchase carried repurchase options for Salt River or its assignee, such as Transwestern Pipeline, that could not be used before April 1, 2008.{b13_23}
drafts.P8263:
Kinder Morgan Tejas Pipeline LLC announced on July 12, 2023, that it had signed the binding commercial agreements needed for the project, at a cost of about $251 million. It was built alongside a 62 mile, 36 inch pipeline from Webb County to Freer by Dos Caminos, a joint venture of Howard Energy Partners. Together the projects would carry up to 2 billion cubic feet per day of Eagle Ford gas to Gulf Coast markets. Both were planned for completion in the fourth quarter of 2023.{b13_24}

Kinder Morgan described the line as a supply link for growth with power generators, industrial customers and LNG exporters on its Texas intrastate network.{b13_24}
